newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan hails Canada's return of murder suspects.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan hails Canada's return of murder suspects.

text.p: Taipei on Wednesday welcomed Canada's decision to return six Taiwanese sailors for trial in Taiwan on charges they put three Romanian stowaways overboard to perish on the high seas.
"The decision not only complies with international laws and practices, but also shows Canada's respect for our judicial system," foreign ministry spokesman Peter Cheng told reporters.

State television quoted foreign ministry officials as claiming a small victory for Taiwan's exiled and diplomatically isolated Republic of China government because Canada agreed to accept Taiwan's jurisdiction over the case.
Canada does not recognise Taiwan's government but only the communist People's Republic of China in Beijing, which also claimed sovereignty over the case.
Beijing has regarded the island as a rebel province rather than sovereign nation since a civil war split them in 1949.

In a statement from Ottawa, Canadian Justice Minister Allan Rock said the seamen, all officers of the merchant ship Maersk Dubai, were expected to leave Canada on Thursday to face prosecution in Taiwan.

Rock said the decision to send the sailors home was made after Taiwan authorities gave Canada assurances that the evidence would be fully reviewed and the men would face prosecution in Taipei for their alleged crimes.
Taiwan Justice Minister Liao Cheng-hao said prosecutors would begin investigating immediately the seamen arrived.
"We will question the six sailors. We will start investigation after their arrival," Liao told reporters.
The six officers have been part of a year-long diplomatic tussle between Canada, Romania, Taiwan and China.
Earlier in March, Nova Scotia Supreme Court Judge Michael MacDonald freed the sailors on grounds he did not have authority to order their extradition to Romania on murder charges.
The officers were not allowed to leave Canada pending an appeal.
In his ruling, MacDonald nevertheless said enough evidence was presented during a 41-day extradition hearing to warrant murder and manslaughter charges against the seamen.
Acting on behalf of Romania, Canada was seeking to extradite the officers to Bucharest. Taiwan opposed the extradition and finally offered to prosecute the men in Taipei.

During the Canadian extradition hearing, Filipino crewmen testified that the Taiwan officers put two Romanian stowaways overboard to their presumed deaths off the Spanish coast in March 1996. On another voyage in May, one Romanian stowaway on the ship was also put overboard.
The missing stowaways' bodies were never found. Authorities in Bucharest said the men's families had not heard from them.
